To canonize something or someone means to officially declare them to be of the highest, most authoritative status — to formally place them in a special, elevated category that a recognized authority or community accepts as final and definitive.

The key word here is officially. Canonizing is not just admiring or praising something. It is a formal, authoritative act of declaring: "This belongs in the highest tier. This is accepted. This is real and recognized."
The Religious Meaning (Its Most Precise Use)

The most specific and original use of "canonize" is in the Catholic Church (and some other Christian traditions). Here, to canonize someone means for the Church to officially and formally declare that a deceased person is a saint.

This is not a casual opinion. It is a solemn, final declaration made by the Pope after a long, rigorous investigation into the person's life, their virtues, and miracles attributed to them. Once a person is canonized, they are permanently placed on the Church's official list of recognized saints — called the canon of saints — and the entire Church acknowledges them as a saint forever.

"The Pope canonized Mother Teresa in 2016, and she became officially known as Saint Teresa of Calcutta."

Before this happened, millions of people already admired and revered her. But admiration is not canonization. Canonization is when the highest authority makes it official and permanent.
Understanding "Canon" — The Word Behind the Word

To truly understand "canonize," you need to know what a canon is, because to canonize literally means to place something into the canon.

A canon is simply the officially accepted, authoritative collection or list in a particular field. Think of it as "the official roster of what counts as the best or the real thing."

A few examples:

  • The biblical canon = the officially accepted books of the Bible (as decided by the Church)
  • The literary canon = the collection of books that scholars and academics consider the most essential and greatest in literature
  • The canon of saints = the Church's official list of recognized saints

So when you canonize something, you are placing it into that authoritative list. You are stamping it with: "This officially belongs among the greatest. This is accepted at the highest level."

Over time, "canonize" moved well beyond religion. Today, people use it in literature, art, music, film, and culture to mean: to officially elevate something to the highest, most respected, most authoritative status in its field — to the point where it is treated as a gold standard.

  • Shakespeare has been canonized as the greatest writer in the English language — meaning the academic and literary world has collectively, authoritatively agreed that his work sits at the very top.
  • Beethoven has been canonized in classical music — the world treats his compositions as the ultimate standard of the art form.
  • Certain films, books, or albums get canonized when critics, scholars, and institutions consistently place them at the top of "greatest of all time" lists, making their greatness feel like an established, authoritative fact rather than just one person's opinion.
The Critical Nuance: Official and Authoritative, Not Just Popular

This is the most important thing to understand about this word.

Canonizing ≠ praising or celebrating.

Many people can love and praise something. But that alone does not canonize it. What separates canonization from mere appreciation is authority and formal recognition — by an institution, a scholarly community, a church, or a very powerful cultural consensus built over a long time.

Think of it this way:

  • A student saying "I think Shakespeare is the greatest writer" → This is personal admiration.
  • The entire global literary and academic world agreeing for centuries that Shakespeare belongs at the absolute top of literature, including him in every serious curriculum, and treating his greatness as settled fact → This is canonization.

The difference is the presence of authority, formality, and broad consensus.
When "Canonize" Carries a Critical or Negative Tone

Sometimes people use this word to criticize the act of over-elevating something. When someone says, "Critics have canonized this author," they might mean it negatively — suggesting that people treat the author as untouchable and beyond criticism, almost sacred, in a way that is excessive or unfair.

In this negative use, canonizing means putting something on such a high pedestal that questioning it feels almost like a sin. This can be unhealthy — in literature, it can mean newer or less celebrated writers get ignored; in religion, it can imply blind, uncritical worship.

So the tone of "canonize" depends on context:

  • Neutral tone → Simply stating a fact about official recognition. ("The Church canonized him in 1950.")
  • Positive tone → Celebrating the elevation of something truly great. ("This album has rightfully been canonized as a masterpiece.")
  • Critical tone → Implying that something is being treated with excessive, uncritical reverence. ("This overrated novel has been canonized by academics who refuse to question it.")

• "The Pope canonized the new saints in a grand ceremony." → Formally declared them saints (religious use).
  • "Orwell's 1984 has been canonized as one of the greatest novels of the 20th century." → Officially elevated to the top tier of literature.
  • "The art world has canonized Picasso to the point where critics rarely dare challenge his legacy." → Elevated to untouchable status (slightly critical tone).
  • "These five films were canonized by film schools and critics as essential cinema." → Officially recognized as part of the authoritative collection of the greatest films.

To canonize something means to officially and authoritatively declare it to be of the highest, most accepted, most sacred status — whether by a church formally recognizing a saint, or by a culture collectively agreeing that something belongs among the greatest of its kind.
